findings.title: The pericope's dependencies close in praise
findings.claim: Against the pericope's scenes of failed protection, re-creation, human hoarding, and coercive rule, the focus's three denials gather distinct forms of dependence: inherited child, shared dominion, and a protector required because of abasement. Its praise and final magnification close those relations around one undivided referent.
findings.mechanism: The focus's self-taking verb and child meet the renewed creation of 17:98-99; partner and dominion meet the hypothetical human ownership of mercy's stores in 17:100 and the Pharaoh sequence in 17:101-104; protector and abasement meet the unavailable allies of 17:97 and the voluntary lowering of 17:107-109. The preceding names and calibrated address in 17:110 then meet the focus's praise and takbir, so the contextual contacts change the three negations from a bare list into a closing account of non-dependent rule.
findings.reader_payoff: The final praise now gathers the pericope's contrasting dependencies into one ending: the creature seeks guidance, human ownership fears depletion, and coercive rule cannot secure land, while the focus denies lineage, co-rule, and protective repair before magnifying God.
findings.containment: These are contextual analogies, not identifications of the verse with any one episode. The focus still says praise belongs to Allah, that He has no child, no partner in dominion, and no ally arising from abasement, followed by a command to magnify Him. The qualified KBR facet is used for upward greatness, not human arrogance.

epistemic.reason: The focus carriers have registered branch facets and the native context surfaces are supplied exactly; the unifying pericope relation remains an interpretive synthesis of trusted nominations.

findings.title: The direction of protection reverses
findings.claim: Before the pericope is brought alongside it, the focus can sound like a bare denial that God has a protector. In context, 17:97 says creatures depend on divine guidance and cannot find allies apart from Him, while the focus denies that He needs an ally because of abasement.
findings.mechanism: The focus wali carries supportive alliance and al-dhull carries the vulnerability that could call for protection. The independent 17:97 guidance, failed search for allies, and apart-from-Him phrase meet those carriers and reverse the dependency direction: creatures seek protection from God; God is not a vulnerable being whose sovereignty must be repaired by a protector.
findings.reader_payoff: The shared protective relation has a direction: the creature seeks support from God, while the focus removes need in the reverse direction.
findings.containment: The HFT alternative remains live: each clause may reject false patrons locally without constructing a full protector/protected reversal. The comparison does not make God's relation to creatures identical to creaturely protection.

epistemic.reason: The exact context indices and roots match the packet and the focus return is QAC-grounded; HFT segmentation and roles remain attributed because context morphology is not supplied.

findings.mechanism: The focus's literal walad is the carrier. The independent creation-after-rupture, renewed creation, capacity, and likeness occurrences in 17:98-99 activate an analogical relation between something deriving from another and creation that does not require lineage.

Here the literal child is the comparison pole; it is not claimed that walad lexically means a manufactured thing. The HFT alternative also remains live: the clause may deny offspring without implying a theory of production.

findings.title: Unshared dominion and human scarcity
findings.claim: Before 17:100 enters, the focus's no-partner clause can remain an abstract claim about exclusive rule. The pericope's human owner fears spending and withholds mercy; against that chain, unshared dominion also means mercy is not administered by a scarcity-bound co-owner.
findings.mechanism: The focus al-mulk carries rule and possession. In 17:100 the human possession of mercy's stores is paired with holding back, fear of expenditure, and constriction. Those separate occurrences meet the focus carrier and change the denial from a count of rulers into a contrast between unshared dominion and scarcity-conditioned co-management.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader sees what the focus's no-partner clause does beside the human counterexample: it closes the possibility that a co-owner's fear of loss can ration the domain.
findings.containment: The live alternative remains: 17:100 may criticize human parsimony without explaining why divine dominion has no partner. The focus does not call mercy a literal treasury or explicitly mention expenditure.

epistemic.reason: All cited 17:100 roots and indices are supplied and match the HFT trace; the move from human scarcity to divine dominion is an attributed contextual inference.

findings.title: Coercive rule is reversed
findings.claim: Before 17:103-104 is set beside the focus, the unpartnered dominion can read as abstract exclusivity. The pericope stages Pharaoh's confrontation, his attempted displacement of a people, and its reversal into drowning, settlement, and later gathering; the focus then reads as a judgment on coercive rule that cannot secure its project.
findings.mechanism: The focus al-mulk carries sovereign rule. The HFT-attributed displacement and drowning in 17:103, followed by settlement and gathering in 17:104, provide the independent contact; 17:101-102 identify the contest with Pharaoh and the Lord of the heavens and earth. Their relation changes the focus from an abstract no-partner statement into a contextual contrast between lasting sovereignty and coercive possession.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader sees the final sovereignty claim against an attempted expulsion whose outcome reverses the ruler's project.
findings.containment: The live alternative remains that 17:103-104 recount historical acts without an institutional gloss. The Pharaoh sequence is a contextual analogy for the focus, not its exclusive referent or a claim about a later ruler.

epistemic.reason: All HFT word indices and roots in 17:103-104 match the supplied context; the political judgment is an attributed inference, and 17:101-102 supply the episode frame.

branch_activations.facet_statement: Hükümdar, halk üzerinde emir ve yasak koyarak kamusal yönetim yetkisi kullanır.
branch_activations.carrier: Al-mulk carries the public domain of rule.
branch_activations.independent_trigger: Pharaoh's challenge and failed expulsion are followed by drowning, settlement, and gathering.
branch_activations.activation: The focus's carrier of rule meets the explicit reversal of a coercer's project and the adjacent statement naming the Lord of the heavens and earth.
branch_activations.resulting_reading: The denial of a divine partner also reads as a contrast between durable rule and coercive possession that cannot secure its aim.
branch_activations.boundary: The political effect is attributed and does not make the historical episode the sole meaning of al-mulk.

findings.title: Magnification meets voluntary lowering
findings.claim: Before 17:107 and 17:109 enter, takbir may sound chiefly like an upward verbal assertion. The focus's greatness now meets knowledgeable listeners who fall, prostrate, and grow in humility; the upward recognition and the worshipper's voluntary bodily lowering become one vertical relation.
findings.mechanism: The focus KBR carrier names magnification, while al-dhull names the coerced abasement denied of God. In 17:107 the knowers fall and prostrate; in 17:109 they fall again and their khushu increases. That separate bodily and affective sequence activates the contrast between divine greatness and a worshipper lowering in response.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can see humility growing as a response to recognition of greatness, with the focus's denial of coercive abasement still intact.
findings.containment: The live alternative remains that the adjacent devotional acts stand independently. The relation does not equate coerced abasement with voluntary prostration or claim that every form of lowliness is worshipful.

epistemic.reason: The four context coordinates match the supplied roots and the two focus occurrences match QAC; the vertical reciprocity is an attributed HFT inference.

findings.title: The relations of a fragile regime fall away
findings.claim: Before the political analogy, the focus's three denials can be read as metaphysical exclusions alone. Its child, partner in dominion, and wali relations also map onto the fragile supports of a regime: dynasty, co-rule, and emergency patronage, all unnecessary to divine sovereignty.
findings.mechanism: The focus child supplies dynastic continuity, sharik supplies multi-party participation, al-mulk makes rule explicit, and the focus wali can carry administrative guardianship. The independent 17:103 attempt at displacement and 17:104 settlement reverse a coercive sovereign project; that contact makes the focus's relation slots legible as a political analogy about rule that does not require an heir, co-regent, or emergency guardian.
findings.reader_payoff: A familiar architecture of fragile rule becomes newly visible in the focus's three negations, while the preceding territorial reversal tests how little force can secure.
findings.containment: This remains the supplied surprising political analogy, not the verse's exclusive referent, a historical identification, or a claim that child, partner, and wali always name regime institutions. The alternative remains the plain metaphysical list.

epistemic.reason: The exact focus and context coordinates agree with the packet, but the political mapping is explicitly exploratory and remains attributed to a legacy-unbound HFT trace.
